title: What We Learned by Reproducing 2,200 papers from ICML
gist: A 19-day Hugging Face/alphaXiv hackathon put 1,221 community members and their coding agents against 2,226 accepted ICML 2026 papers (34% of the conference), judging 35,908 individual claims: 51% of examined papers had at least one claim verified, 23% had at least one claim falsified or contested, and 242 papers drew opposite verdicts from independent teams. The same agent technology inflating submission volume (23,918 submissions, roughly double the prior year) is now the only thing that can audit it at scale, but the most reliable results still came from human-steered workflows.

insights.claim: ICML 2026 received 23,918 submissions and accepted 6,352 papers, roughly double the previous year, continuing an exponential trend the author attributes at least partly to AI agents making experiments faster to run and write up.
insights.speaker: Abubakar Abid
insights.so_what: Peer-reviewed paper counts are no longer a proxy for validated research output; any diligence process that treats 'published at a top conference' as a quality gate is being silently diluted at ~2x per year.
insights.quote: ICML 2026 received 23,918 submissions and accepted 6,352 papers, roughly double the previous year, continuing an exponential trend that is at least partly driven by AI agents making it faster to run experiments and write them up.
insights.locator: More papers than anyone can review

insights.claim: Reviewing capacity at ML conferences has not scaled with submissions because reviewers are volunteers who may lack the time or expertise to fully review a paper, producing accepted spotlight papers whose reviewers explicitly admit to not checking the proofs.
insights.speaker: Abubakar Abid
insights.so_what: The bottleneck in ML research quality is verification labor, not idea generation — a structural opening for automated verification tooling and for skepticism toward headline benchmark claims.
insights.quote: "My low confidence score is because I did not check all the proofs carefully."
insights.locator: Reviewing capacity has not doubled along with it

insights.claim: The economics of paper verification have inverted: what used to cost a human reviewer a weekend can now be attempted by a coding agent in an afternoon, in parallel, thousands of times over.
insights.speaker: Abubakar Abid
insights.so_what: Verification cost collapsing by ~1000x in parallel throughput makes large-scale adversarial auditing of scientific and commercial claims newly viable as a product category.
insights.quote: Checking a paper carefully used to cost a reviewer a weekend; an agent can attempt it in an afternoon, in parallel, thousands of times over.
insights.locator: What has changed, though, is that

insights.claim: The same technology driving the flood of low-verification submissions is the technology capable of absorbing it, making agent-driven auditing a self-correcting response to agent-driven paper production rather than a separate intervention.
insights.speaker: Abubakar Abid
insights.so_what: Expect audit/verification tooling to grow in lockstep with generative research volume — a durable secondary market attached to the primary agent boom.

themes.theme: Audit design that made it work

insights.claim: Organizers pre-indexed all 6,341 accepted ICML 2026 papers and extracted each one's core scientific claims so agents could start from a concrete checkable target instead of a 40-page PDF, which was the key enabler for agent-driven reproduction at scale.
insights.speaker: Abubakar Abid
insights.so_what: Claim-level decomposition is the reusable primitive for any agentic verification product — the same pattern applies to auditing financial filings, clinical trials, or vendor benchmarks.
insights.quote: We indexed all 6,341 accepted ICML 2026 papers with their abstracts and extracted the core scientific claims of each one, so an agent could start from a concrete, checkable target rather than a 40-page PDF.
insights.locator: Pick a paper.

insights.claim: Every reproduction attempt was published as a Trackio logbook — a static Hugging Face Space carrying the write-up, the code, the artifacts, and optionally the full agent execution trace as a Hugging Face Dataset — on the explicit principle that the auditing process itself had to be auditable.
insights.speaker: Abubakar Abid
insights.so_what: Publishing agent traces as first-class artifacts is becoming the trust mechanism for agentic work; platforms that host traces capture the audit layer of the AI stack.
insights.quote: The auditing process itself had to be auditable.
insights.locator: Reproduce, then publish everything.

insights.claim: An automated Logbook Judge running the open-weights model GLM-5.2 re-read every logbook and issued per-claim verdicts of verified, falsified, toy, or inconclusive, and was explicitly instructed to treat each logbook's self-assessment as untrusted.
insights.speaker: Abubakar Abid
insights.so_what: A flagship open-weights model was trusted as the adjudication layer for 35,908 claims — evidence that open models are now good enough for high-volume evaluation workloads that would otherwise route to frontier APIs.
insights.quote: The judge was explicitly instructed to treat each logbook's self-assessment as untrusted.
insights.locator: Get judged.

insights.claim: Participants were given only $20 each in Hugging Face compute credits and still launched 2,962 cloud jobs on HF Jobs across the challenge, showing that meaningful reproduction work now sits at a trivial per-unit compute cost.
insights.speaker: Abubakar Abid
insights.so_what: The marginal cost of an agent-run scientific audit is now in the tens of dollars, which removes budget as the constraint on mass verification and shifts the bottleneck to orchestration and judgment.
insights.quote: Participants received $20 in Hugging Face compute credits to run experiments on HF Jobs; across the challenge, participants launched 2,962 cloud jobs.
insights.locator: Participants received $20 in Hugging Face compute credits

insights.claim: Where full reproduction was impossible because a paper's dataset was proprietary or its checkpoints unreleased, participants ran 'toy' reproductions on synthetic data mimicking the original's properties, and the judge scored these as a distinct verdict class rather than as verification.
insights.speaker: Abubakar Abid
insights.so_what: Closed artifacts systematically downgrade a paper's verifiability — a reason to discount claims from labs that withhold data and weights, and a tailwind for open-artifact norms.
insights.locator: Where a full reproduction was impossible

insights.claim: Rather than auditing centrally, Hugging Face crowdsourced the effort to 1,221 community members bringing heterogeneous agent frameworks, compute budgets and scientific taste — including Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and OpenResearch's orx — deliberately treating framework diversity as a feature of the audit.
insights.speaker: Abubakar Abid
insights.so_what: Ensemble-of-heterogeneous-agents is emerging as the credible verification architecture; single-vendor agent monocultures inherit correlated blind spots.
insights.quote: Rather than audit papers ourselves, we opened it up to the whole community, with all the diversity of agent frameworks, compute budgets, and scientific taste that brings.
insights.locator: The hackathon (July 15 - August 2nd)

insights.claim: In 19 days, 6,816 reproduction logbooks were published covering 2,226 papers — about 34% of an entire major ML conference — with 35,908 individual claims judged and all verdicts frozen in a public dataset at close.
insights.speaker: Abubakar Abid
insights.so_what: A public, frozen, claim-level verdict dataset over a third of a top conference is a novel training and evaluation corpus for research-verification models — watch who builds on it.
insights.quote: In 19 days, participants published 6,816 Trackio logbooks reproducing 2,226 papers, about a third of the conference
insights.locator: Back in July, we ran a hackathon

insights.claim: 51% of examined ICML 2026 papers (1,103) had at least one claim independently verified, but only 266 papers were fully reproduced with every extracted claim verified — meaning under a quarter of examined papers cleared the full bar.
insights.speaker: Abubakar Abid
insights.so_what: Roughly 12% of the examined slice of a flagship ML conference is fully verified end-to-end — a base rate to apply when a startup or vendor cites accepted-paper provenance as evidence.
insights.quote: 51% of examined papers (1,103) had at least one claim independently verified. Of those, 266 papers were fully reproduced, with every extracted claim verified
insights.locator: What we found

insights.claim: 23% of examined papers (496) had at least one claim falsified or contested, including 49 papers where every claim was falsified and nothing could be verified at all.
insights.speaker: Abubakar Abid
insights.so_what: A near-one-in-four contest rate on accepted papers argues for independent replication before building product or capital allocation on any single published ML result.
insights.quote: 23% of examined papers (496) had at least one claim falsified or contested.
insights.locator: What we found

insights.claim: 242 papers had independent reproduction teams reach opposite verdicts on the same claims, which the author reads as evidence that reproducibility is not a binary property but an adversarial process.
insights.speaker: Abubakar Abid
insights.so_what: Single-shot replication attempts, human or agentic, are unreliable signals; treat verification like an adversarial market where the number of independent attempts is the quality variable.
insights.quote: Reproducibility is not binary; it is adversarial.
insights.locator: What we found

insights.claim: 502 examined papers yielded only toy-scale evidence and 280 had nothing established either way, with missing artifacts the most common cause of an inconclusive verdict.
insights.speaker: Abubakar Abid
insights.so_what: Artifact release policy is the single biggest lever on whether a result can be checked at all — a concrete metric for evaluating the credibility of any AI lab's published work.
insights.quote: 280 where nothing could be established either way (missing artifacts were the most common cause)
insights.locator: The remainder sat in the middle

insights.claim: Papers that survive mass adversarial replication do exist and are identifiable: 'Flat Minima and Generalization: Insights from Stochastic Convex Optimization' was reproduced by 20 independent teams with 12 verifying every claim, and 'A Coin Flip for Safety: LLM Judges Fail to Reliably Measure Adversarial Robustness' had 14 of 17 logbooks verify every claim.
insights.speaker: Abubakar Abid
insights.so_what: Replication-count-and-verification-rate becomes a usable quality score per paper, letting practitioners rank literature by evidence weight rather than venue prestige.
insights.locator: Reproductions done well

insights.claim: Only 35 participants formally claimed a falsification, and every claimed falsification was adversarially re-verified by re-reading the paper and logbook and re-deriving the math or re-implementing the experiment from the paper's own text.
insights.speaker: Abubakar Abid
insights.so_what: Formal falsification is rare and expensive even when reproduction is cheap — the scarce resource is the willingness and rigor to press a disagreement, not compute.
insights.quote: 35 participants formally claimed they had falsified something. We adversarially re-verified every claimed falsification
insights.locator: Falsifications, and what happened when we checked them

insights.claim: The ICML spotlight paper 'Towards Optimal Robustness in Learning-Augmented Paging' — whose reviewer admitted not checking the proofs — had its claimed additive robustness term shown to grow logarithmically rather than as O(1), with the organizers' own re-implementation extending the sweep to k = 1,024 and confirming the growth at roughly nine sigma.
insights.speaker: Abubakar Abid
entities: Towards Optimal Robustness in Learning-Augmented Paging
insights.so_what: A spotlight-tier theory result was wrong in its headline bound and nobody caught it in review — the strongest single data point that venue signal does not equal correctness.
insights.locator: The paging paper from the introduction.

insights.claim: In 'Attention's forward pass and Frank-Wolfe', three independent teams found counterexamples to a collapse theorem with violations first appearing only at t = 224, ~3,800, and 6,416 steps, explaining why other teams 'verified' the claim — finite-horizon checks stopped too early.
insights.speaker: Abubakar Abid
insights.so_what: Horizon length is a systematic blind spot in agentic verification; any benchmark or eval with a fixed short budget will over-report success on scale-dependent behavior.
insights.quote: which neatly explains why everyone else "verified" the claim: finite-horizon checks stop too early.
insights.locator: A theorem that falls after step 224.

insights.claim: In 'Self-Distillation Enables Continual Learning', the paper's central equation and entire theory section analyze reverse KL divergence while the released code's default — which per the authors produced all the paper's results — computes forward KL, and the logbook that caught it also failed to reproduce the headline +4pp result under the authors' own code and data.
insights.speaker: Abubakar Abid
insights.so_what: Theory-code mismatch is a distinct and detectable failure class that pure numeric replication misses; agents reading both the math and the repo catch what benchmark reruns cannot.
insights.locator: Theory written for one loss, results produced by another.

insights.claim: In 'Do Transformers Need Three Projections?', roughly 66% of evaluated label positions were EOS padding tokens that train to near-zero loss, deflating reported perplexity about threefold and turning the abstract's '3.1% quality cost for 50% cache reduction' into roughly 9.4% once corrected.
insights.speaker: Abubakar Abid
insights.so_what: Evaluation-harness artifacts can inflate efficiency-vs-quality tradeoffs by ~3x — directly relevant when assessing inference-cost-reduction claims that underpin AI infrastructure economics.
insights.quote: The abstract's "3.1% quality cost for 50% cache reduction" becomes roughly 9.4% once corrected.
insights.locator: An evaluation diluted by padding.

insights.claim: Agent-produced falsifications are themselves unreliable: one logbook dramatically claimed a paper's method was 2x slower than baseline, but this was an arithmetic bug comparing per-trajectory time against per-batch-of-50 time, and correctly normalized the participant's own data confirmed the paper's claimed 8x speedup.
insights.speaker: Abubakar Abid
insights.so_what: Agentic audit output needs its own adversarial review layer — deploying agents as unsupervised critics manufactures false negatives as readily as it catches real errors.
insights.quote: this turned out to be an arithmetic bug in the reproduction: per-trajectory time compared against per-batch-of-50 time.
insights.locator: False falsifications.

insights.claim: Authors have responded to confirmed findings positively rather than defensively, with confirmations on multiple papers, two arXiv corrections in flight, and one case where an author had quietly fixed the error in a new arXiv version a month before the challenge independently found it.
insights.speaker: Abubakar Abid
insights.so_what: Low social friction on agent-found corrections suggests mass automated auditing can be normalized quickly rather than being blocked by community resistance.
insights.quote: in one case an author had quietly fixed the error in a new arXiv version a month before the challenge found it, which we count as independent convergence
insights.locator: Talking to authors

insights.claim: Pure agent execution hit real limits in the challenge: agents got stuck in local loops, misread scale-dependent behavior, and occasionally built an entire falsification on top of a units mismatch.
insights.speaker: Abubakar Abid
insights.so_what: Concrete, observed failure taxonomy for autonomous research agents — useful for underwriting claims that agents can run science unsupervised.
insights.quote: Agents got stuck in local loops, misread scale-dependent behavior
insights.locator: Pure agent execution hits real limits.

insights.claim: The challenge's most reliable results came from workflows where a human was steering — re-pointing the agent, questioning an assumption, or deciding an experiment's premise was wrong before burning a week of compute on it.
insights.speaker: Abubakar Abid
insights.so_what: Value accrues to human-steering tooling and interfaces, not to fully autonomous research pipelines, at least at this capability level.
insights.quote: The challenge's most reliable results came from workflows where a human was steering
insights.locator: Pure agent execution hits real limits.

insights.claim: Some evaluation remains irreducibly human: the human-in-the-loop winner examined a paper claiming stable image generation under extreme quantization where numerical metrics said 'no collapse' but usability was perceptual, so the agent built a purpose-built review UI and the human personally judged all 128 image pairs with annotations committed to the repo.
insights.speaker: Abubakar Abid
insights.so_what: Where the ground truth is perceptual, metric-only claims can pass while the artifact is unusable — a recurring trap in quantization and compression marketing.
insights.quote: Numerical metrics said "no collapse"; whether the images were actually usable was a perceptual question.
insights.locator: Some evaluation is irreducibly human, for now.

insights.claim: The author's model for the human role in agentic research is the principal investigator: humans should manage intelligence by building the right environment — compute, harnesses, data access and targeted feedback at the right moments — and asking the right questions, then let agents do the running.
insights.speaker: Abubakar Abid
insights.so_what: If the PI analogy holds, the durable AI-era skill and product surface is environment/harness construction and evaluation design, not prompt-level task execution.
insights.quote: So what are our roles as human reviewers? We think it is to manage intelligence effectively.
insights.locator: The role of humans
